1.pericope_label: Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation... they bless with their mouth, but they curse inwardly

schools.summary: Take the opening as a noun, not a verb: Ellicott gives 'unto God (is) silence my soul', insists 'defence' is properly a high tower set against the tottering wall of the next verse, and lays out the renderings of the verb that occurs only here. Delitzsch dates the psalm to Absalom's rebellion and pairs it with the thirty-ninth.

Read the silence as achieved rather than native. Calvin makes it 'patient silence' won against a curbed impatience, and doubts the psalm was given to Jeduthun at all; Gill distinguishes silence as to murmuring from silence as to prayer, and keeps both Saul's persecution and Absalom's in view.

Clarke rejects the English rendering outright for 'Surely to God only is my soul dumb', reaches the assault-sense of the rare verb independently, and finds in it the riotous manner of the rebellion; Wesley hears the third verse as an appeal from a man to men of his own kind.

Spurgeon takes the first word for 'only' and makes the silence a work of grace — wax to the Lord, adamant to every other force; Henry glosses the waiting soul as one that 'says nothing against what he does, but quietly expects what he will do'.
Augustine reads the title's name as a leaping over and the psalm as spoken from a height, where the danger is not the enemy below but pride.

debates.question: How should the first clause be rendered?

positions.view: As silence: 'only to God is my soul silence', or dumb, or patiently still — Clarke holding that 'the original will not warrant' the received 'waiteth upon God'.
As subjection, with the ancient versions: 'Shall not my soul be subject to God?'

debates.question: What does the name in the title signify?

positions.view: The chief of the family band of singers, to whom the psalm was sent.
Not a dedication at all; the words may have opened 'some song commonly known at that time'.
A meaning rather than a man — a leaping over, which sets the psalmist on a height above those he has passed.

debates.question: What does the verb of the third verse mean?

positions.view: To storm or assault, from the Arabic root — preferable to the Rabbinical 'imagine mischief' and to 'plot against' or 'labour in vain'.

outliers.view: The only voice to make the psalm's danger internal — the height gained by leaping over others being itself the occasion of pride.

themes: Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation.
He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved.
How long will ye imagine mischief against a man? ye shall be slain all of you: as a bowing wall shall ye be, and as a tottering fence.
They only consult to cast him down from his excellency: they delight in lies: they bless with their mouth, but they curse inwardly. Selah.

5.pericope_label: My soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him... Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the seventh verse's preposition literally, 'upon God', and names prayer as the only thing that preserves the state of resignation; Delitzsch alone treats the section structurally, finding in the earthly form of the new kingship the germ of its own ruin.

Gill supplies an occasion for the self-address — a fresh temptation, since 'frames are very changeable things' — and defines the commanded trust by everything it excludes, riches, wisdom, strength, birth, the law and one's own righteousness alike.
Clarke turns waiting into surrender, 'resign thyself into his hands', and reads the eighth verse politically, as a loyalist's rallying cry with the usurper's fall attached.

Spurgeon guards against relapse and against divided reliance — faith with a single eye sees herself secure, but two confidences blind her; Henry opens the exhortation to all people and distinguishes habitual trust from actual, and the drink-offering sense of pouring out from the praying sense.

debates.question: Who are the 'people' told to trust?

positions.view: All people. 'All shall be welcome to trust in God' — though the Chaldee restricts the address to the house of Israel.
The covenant people: those 'that are Israelites indeed'.
The king's loyal subjects, addressed as a political party: 'all ye who are faithful to your king'.

debates.question: What is it to pour out the heart?

positions.view: The phrase alludes to the drink-offerings and covers penitent confession, but is meant here of prayer — laying grievances before God and then referring oneself to his disposal.

outliers.view: The only voice to read the passage as argument rather than devotion, making it the hinge at which God decides as Judge 'between the dethroned and the usurpers'.

themes: My soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him.
He only is my rock and my salvation: he is my defence; I shall not be moved.
In God is my salvation and my glory: the rock of my strength, and my refuge, is in God.
Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah.

9.pericope_label: Surely men of low degree are vanity, and men of high degree are a lie... thou renderest to every man according to his work

schools.summary: Ellicott renders vanity as 'mere breath', agrees that the balance is idiom, and prefers a one-letter emendation giving 'when weighed in the scales'; he takes 'once; twice' as the usual Hebrew way of emphasising a number in a verse that 'loves a climax', and extends the tenth verse's warning even to honest wealth.

Gill distrusts the poor as much as the rich, since the wicked poor are 'of all persons, the most wicked'; he reads 'once' as finality rather than frequency — what God has once spoken 'is irreversible and immutable' — and takes mercy as the second thing heard.

Clarke carries the philology of the two words for man, declares that almost every version and commentary has missed the eleventh verse, and reads the tenth against his own son's partisans; Wesley keeps to the plain sense, that power is God's prerogative and mercy the answer to a good man's failings.
Spurgeon presses the psalm's 'only' again, finds the crowd that cries Hosanna and then crucify, and judges the high worse than the low precisely because more was expected of them.

positions.view: God spoke once and two truths were heard — that he is the Origin of power and the Fountain of mercy. 'Almost every version, translation, and commentary has missed the sense.'
A rhetorical form, not a count: the usual Hebrew way of emphasising a numerical statement in a verse that builds to a climax.
Not a limit on God's speaking, which has been frequent, but a statement of its finality — or simply of its repetition, at Sinai and by the prophets.

debates.question: Does the balance clause need emending?

positions.view: No. The Hebrew as it stands is idiom — 'in the balances they ascend', exactly our 'they kick the beam'.
Probably. 'A slight change in one letter gives the more probable, when weighed in the scales.'

outliers.view: The only voice to rank the classes against each other, making men of high degree worse than the multitude because expectation of them is higher and the disappointment total.

themes: Surely men of low degree are vanity, and men of high degree are a lie: to be laid in the balance, they are altogether lighter than vanity.
Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.
God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God.
Also unto thee, O Lord, belongeth mercy: for thou renderest to every man according to his work.
